title: Competence is Queen
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart pivots from credibility-signaling strategies to the substance behind them: actual teaching competence. He argues there's no shortcut to competence, only faster and slower paths, and the fastest path is focusing deliberate practice on a short list of areas that matter most — cultivating student motivation, managing behavior, delivering useful instruction, giving timely feedback, helping stuck students, explaining clearly, and staying organized. He warns against several time-sinks that feel like growth but aren't: chasing trending strategies, adopting someone else's complicated systems, obsessing over evaluation rubrics, and using strategies mindlessly without understanding why they work. He closes with three concrete methods for improvement — watching other teachers, recording and reviewing your own teaching, and exhaustively mining a few trusted sources rather than skimming many.
points: Stuart's central move is separating credibility (signaling you're good at your job) from competence (actually being good at it), insisting both matter but competence is the substance behind the signal.

His seven focus areas for competence — motivation, behavior management, instruction, timely feedback, helping stuck students, clear explanation, and organization — function as a deliberate-practice checklist rather than a generic 'be a good teacher' exhortation.
He specifically warns that talkative, verbally gifted teachers can mistake their own explaining for productive teaching, when 'whoever is doing the talking is doing most of the thinking.'
His recommended growth methods (watching other teachers, recording yourself, exhaustively mining a few trusted sources) favor depth and imitation over breadth and novelty.
quotes: JK — there's no such thing as a lightning fast path to competence. It takes lots of practice. But — but! — there IS something that gets you to competence a heckuva lot faster than most folks: focusing your practice on the work that matters most.

Do you know how to explain things clearly and succinctly? I've seen more than a few highly talented teachers lean too heavily on their verbal acumen — this can feel like productive teaching, but whoever is doing the talking is doing most of the thinking.
But using someone else's complicated system will almost always shortchange you in growth in competence and cost you a lot of time.

Mindless use of strategies. You should seek to add strategies to your tool belt as you work on building competence. But you should never treat the strategy as if it has some inherent power. The power is in the intelligent use of the tool.
The goal is to internalize the way that the author of the source thinks; you want to create a little AI version of this person in your mind.
You'll never regret investments made in the focused development of teacher competence. Nothing's more predictive of an impactful career.
